overview: The server is the authority for accounts, conversation visibility, messages and durable events. One workspace folder holds SQLite plus attachment blobs; an exclusive writer hold keeps schedulers and storage accounting consistent. The protocol package supplies shared data shapes, request validation and small policies so web, desktop and server agree. Recent work removes redundant private content, contains malformed logging, bounds callback lifetimes and protects delayed replies. The further review's Q01 restore publication race is closed by a path lock held through the folder swap.

entries.plain: Scrambles passwords so they are never saved as typed, and makes the secret keys that keep people signed in.
entries.summary: Derives password credentials and turns bearer tokens into database lookup keys.
details: Passwords use asynchronous scrypt with a fresh 16-byte random salt and a 64-byte derived key; verification compares equal-length buffers with timingSafeEqual.
A new session returns a random 32-byte token to the caller and its SHA-256 hash for storage. Knowing a stored session hash does not provide the original bearer token.
The module contains cryptographic primitives; expiry, deactivation, session revocation and request admission belong to Store and server.ts.

entries.plain: Makes and checks the six-digit codes an authenticator app shows, and the recovery codes for when the phone is gone.
entries.summary: RFC 6238 time-based codes and recovery codes for two-step sign-in, made with node:crypto alone (E11).
details: codeFor is RFC 4226's truncation of an HMAC-SHA1 over a thirty-second time step, six digits long; a test checks the codes RFC 6238 publishes. base32 and fromBase32 carry the twenty-byte key as authenticator apps take it, as RFC 4648 writes it.

checkCode takes a code for now or one step either side, for a clock a little out, and returns the step it answered. A step at or before the last one accepted is refused, so each code works once even inside its window. Codes are compared with timingSafeEqual.
otpauthUri is what the app scans: the key, the issuer "<workspace> on OwnBase" and the handle, with spaces written as %20.

newRecoveryCodes makes ten codes like k7mq-3hxv from letters and digits nobody misreads (no 0, o, 1, l or i). normalRecoveryCode makes a typed one comparable, so case, spaces and the dash do not matter. The server keeps only their SHA-256 hashes.

entries.plain: Makes a complete backup of the workspace and its files, checks it, and puts a backup back in place when the host restores one.
entries.summary: Captures, verifies, inventories and restores portable workspace backups.
details: VACUUM INTO captures a consistent SQLite snapshot including committed WAL content. Only blobs referenced by that snapshot are copied; a disappearing or wrong-sized referenced blob fails capture.

A staged capture is checked before publication. The manifest records schema, counts, SHA-256 checksums and attachment sizes; verification also checks integrity, foreign keys, duplicate names and containment.
inventoryBackup reads older schemas without upgrading them and explains external app destinations, waiting schedules, undelivered events and surviving sessions before a copy is started.
Restore verifies source and staged bytes, moves the old workspace to a superseded folder and publishes the replacement. It preserves the old copy for recovery instead of deleting it.

Q01: restore holds a path lock beside the target through staging, both renames and rollback. The in-folder hold is still released before the renames, since Windows cannot rename a folder with an open file in it, but a concurrent server start or second restore is refused without creating the target.

entries.plain: Lets the server back itself up on a timer into dated folders, keeping the newest few, so a host does not have to remember to.
entries.summary: Schedules verified backups, prunes old ones and reports how they are going.
details: BackupSchedule arms the next backup from the newest dated folder already there, so restarts do not take extra copies and an overdue one runs a minute after start. One runs at a time; a failure is retried within the hour and counted until a backup works.
Only folders named backup-YYYY-MM-DDTHH-MM-SSZ are listed or pruned, so a shared directory loses nothing else. Pruning happens only after a new backup has been verified.

backupInChildProcess runs the CLI's own backup command in a child process, because VACUUM INTO and the integrity check hold the event loop (about 1.6 s for 300 MB). Stopping the server kills the child; the next capture removes its staging.
server.ts holds attachment removals while a copy runs, so a blob the snapshot names is still there when it is copied, and an isolated copy never schedules backups, which would prune the original's.

entries.plain: Turns the text, buttons and forms that Slack-style apps send into what OwnBase can show, leaving out what it cannot.
entries.summary: Converts supported Slack Block Kit payloads into OwnBase's text, buttons and modal fields.
details: Headers, sections, context and dividers flatten into the existing mrkdwn renderer. Explicit nonempty text wins over blocks, matching the expected fallback behavior.
Only buttons from actions blocks become MessageAction records; labels, values and count are bounded, styles normalized and link URLs restricted to HTTP(S).

Modal parsing (INPUT_ELEMENTS) keeps text inputs, single and multiple selects from options, people, conversations or public channels, checkboxes, radio buttons and date and time pickers (E18a). It runs option groups together, caps fields and options at Slack's ceilings, honours starting values, max_selected_items, filter.include and default_to_current_conversation, and reports dropped fields. A view whose every input was dropped is refused rather than presented as a form that lost its questions; one of text alone is kept (E18b), with no submit button unless it names one.

readAnswer checks each submitted answer against its field: options it listed, its limit, an active account, a conversation the submitter can open and the filter allows, a public channel, a real date or time. It returns Slack's state.values entry (selected_options with text, selected_user, selected_date and so on) or the message shown under the field, so the app never sees an answer its form forbids.
This is a deliberate subset adapter, not a complete Slack UI renderer; unsupported controls are omitted.

entries.plain: Briefly remembers which open forms and replies an app is still allowed to use, and forgets them when the server restarts.
entries.summary: Keeps short-lived app permissions in a bounded in-memory map.
details: Response URLs, triggers and open views carry expiresAt; get removes expired values before returning them.
Insertion sweeps expired entries from the oldest end, then evicts oldest entries above the ceiling. Equal lifetime within each map makes early-stop expiration sweeping valid.
Replacing a key moves it to the newest position. Eviction is treated like expiry, so memory cannot grow with every user and integration forever.
These capabilities intentionally disappear on server restart; they are separate from durable messages and event-delivery rows.

entries.plain: Gives every workspace the built-in /shrug and /me commands, even before any app is added.
entries.summary: Provides built-in /shrug and /me commands before any integration is installed.
details: A map holds description, usage hint and a function that returns the message text or null for invalid arguments.
/shrug escapes its backslash and underscores through the shared formatter so the visible arms survive mrkdwn parsing; /me wraps supplied text in italics.
Built-in names are reserved during app command registration, preventing an app from unexpectedly taking over these commands.
A built-in may say inApp: a command the app runs itself, which the server only lists and reserves, answering a client that sends it anyway with that sentence. /poll is one (E6).

entries.plain: Checks the host's startup settings, such as the port and public address, and says clearly what to fix when one is wrong.
entries.summary: Rejects unusable startup settings with actionable messages.
details: Environment settings are read as OWNBASE_<name>, and only under that name.
Port parsing requires a whole number from 0 to 65535; zero requests an available port. Count settings require safe nonnegative integers rather than silently rounded fractions.
Public URLs must use HTTP(S) without credentials, query or fragment because these addresses are handed to apps and shared as links.
Common bind failures are translated into suggestions such as choosing another port or a valid local interface.
keptSettingsNotes says, a line for each, which of --name, --access-policy and --invite-only an owned workspace did not take, and that owners and admins change them in Workspace settings.
parseClaimCode reads OWNBASE_CLAIM_CODE, the code a host gives for claiming a new workspace (P7): 16 to 64 letters, digits, hyphens or underscores, so a link carries it unchanged.

entries.plain: Sets up the workspace's database and upgrades it to the newest layout, keeping a copy of the old one first.
entries.summary: Defines the SQLite schema history and safely opens or upgrades a workspace.
details: SQLite opens with WAL, foreign keys and a busy timeout. All needed migration steps run in one transaction, so failure rolls back to the original schema and releases the file handle.

An existing database receives a consistent pre-upgrade copy before migration by default. Up to three recognized restorable copies are retained; damaged or unrelated files do not displace a usable copy.
Schema 37 removes actions from deleted messages and superseded/purged replay copies, and blanks text/file IDs from sent schedules. Current live buttons and every unsent schedule remain usable.
Indexes support mention lookup, delegated managers and due cleanup/retry work instead of repeated broad scans.
A newer schema is refused by an older build. Logical cleanup affects active database records; it does not promise erasure of historical backups or freed disk bytes.
Schema 39 adds users.status_expires_at, when a status clears itself, or NULL for one kept until changed (UX-61).
Schema 51 adds apps.scopes, a JSON list of Slack scope names (E18c). Apps that existed get every scope there was then, so nothing they did stops; a scope added later must be given.

Schema 40 adds channel_members.starred, one member's star on a conversation (UX-20). It sits on the membership beside muted, so leaving drops it, joining again starts unstarred, and an archived channel keeps it.

Schema 41 adds messages.forwarded_from_id, the message a forward passes on (E1). It has no foreign key, so a forward outlives an original removed with older history, and a partial index lets an edit or deletion find the forwards of one message.

Schema 42 adds link_previews (E2): one row per previewed link of a message, with its position, address, title, description, site name and picture bytes, type and size, and a removed flag the sender sets. UNIQUE(message_id, url), and ON DELETE CASCADE, so purging a message's row takes its previews.
Schema 43 adds thread_follows.muted (E3): a thread one account muted, kept unfollowed when that account replies.

Schema 44 adds reminders (E4): one per account and message, with remind_at and due_at (NULL while it waits), going with the account or the message row, and indexed for the soonest waiting one and for a message's reminders.

Schema 45 adds polls and poll_votes (E6): a poll per message, its choices in order as JSON, multiple, anonymous and closed_at; and one row per choice an account made, keyed by message, account and choice. Both go with the message's row, votes with the account too, and votes are indexed by account for the choices each account is sent.

Schema 46 adds sidebar_sections (E8): one account's own named sections with their position, going with the account, indexed by account and position; and channel_members.section_id, the section a membership is kept in. It has no foreign key, as forwarded_from_id has none: deleting a section clears it in the same change, and a column with one could not be dropped by the upgrade test.

Schema 47 adds profiles (E9): users.time_zone, users.away (set by hand) and users.avatar_version, and user_avatars, one picture's type and bytes per account, going with the account. Removing a picture deletes its row.
Schema 48 adds messages.call_kind (E10): the kind of note the server left about a call, missed, and null on every other message.

Schema 49 adds two-step sign-in (E11): users.two_step_secret (null while it is off) and users.two_step_step, the last time step a code was accepted for; and two_step_codes, an account's recovery codes as SHA-256 hashes with used_at, going with the account.

Schema 50 adds blocking and reporting (E12): user_blocks, whom each account blocked, going with either account; and message_reports, a reason, a note and when each was resolved, by whom and how, going with the message and the reporter. A partial unique index keeps one open report per person per message, so a new one can open once the last is resolved.

entries.plain: Notes the last 500 huddle joins, leaves and connection problems so owners and admins can look into a failed call.
entries.summary: Keeps the latest 500 lines of what happened in huddles, in memory, for the host.
details: Lines are joins, leaves, setups passed on or dropped, and each side's report of its connection; nothing survives a restart, and none is an address, an SDP or anything said in a call.
Read through GET /api/admin/calls by the owner and admins, filtered to conversations the reader can access.

entries.plain: Keeps each app's live connection open, catches it up after a reconnect, and sends each update only to people allowed to see it.
entries.summary: Authenticates sockets, reconstructs state on reconnect and delivers authorized live events.
details: An initial hello checks protocol version, token, account state and forced password change before the socket joins fan-out. The ready snapshot is read completely first.

A reconnect receives authorized missed events when its cursor remains replayable; otherwise the sync contract replaces history. syncVersion 1 ends with a synced marker so clients know catch-up finished.
Public channel events can reach all signed-in readers; private and DM events require current membership. Session authorization is rechecked after admission, including heartbeat and delivery paths.
byUser groups a person's sockets for targeted updates. Presence lists only online accounts, avoiding a second full offline-account listing at every handshake.
Huddles and typing are ephemeral. Signaling relays only between authorized participants in the same huddle; the server carries signaling, not media.

A place in a huddle (a Seat) belongs to the socket that joined. When that socket closes, holdSeat keeps the place for HUDDLE_GRACE_MS (30 s, huddleGraceMs in ServerOptions) without telling the room, even if the person has other devices online; a join from them within it takes the place back quietly, logged as having come back. A join from another of their devices moves the place there and sends the old socket huddle.moved; a leave or signal from a socket that does not hold the place is ignored or dropped, and signals for a place waiting on its device are dropped. Leave, lost access, sign-out and deactivation (revoke) release the place at once.

Socket callbacks contain thrown failures and close the affected connection with a retryable server error. Heartbeats, authentication timeout, payload limits and idempotent close bound abandoned connections.

Writes huddle joins, refusals, departures with their reason, relayed offers and answers, signals it could not pass on and why, and clients' huddle.report summaries to an in-memory CallLog; the ready snapshot advertises huddleReports.
The ready snapshot also advertises stars, so a client offers Star only where it is kept (UX-20).
The ready snapshot advertises workspaceSettings and says accessPolicy, so a client offers Workspace settings' controls only where the server takes them (UX-60).
The ready snapshot advertises workspaceIcon and says iconVersion (or null), so a client offers the icon upload only where the server keeps one, and shows the icon at once (UX-60).
The ready snapshot advertises forwards, so a client offers Forward only where the server keeps what a forward passes on (E1).
The ready snapshot says linkPreviews, whether new messages get previews now, so Workspace settings shows the setting only where the server has it (E2).
The ready snapshot carries this account's reachable reminders, which also says the server keeps them (E4).
The ready snapshot carries pollChoices, what this account chose in each anonymous poll it can still read, which also says the server keeps polls (E6).
The ready snapshot says sharedFiles, that the server lists shared files (E7).
The ready snapshot carries sidebarSections, the account's sections in order, which also says the server keeps them (E8).

Presence (E9): each socket says whether its device is idle. An account is offline with no socket, away when set away by hand or when every socket says idle, and online otherwise. refreshPresence tells everyone only a change, whether an idle message, a socket opening or closing, or away by hand made it; going offline is told as the last socket closes. The ready snapshot says profiles, and its presence map gives away too.

Rings (E10): the first one into a dm or group_dm huddle rings everyone else in it but bots and deactivated accounts, for HUDDLE_RING_MS (30 s, option huddleRingMs). publishHuddle settles it: whoever it rang who is in the huddle answered, and the caller gone ends it. huddle.decline moves someone to declined. huddle.ring tells the caller and everyone rung each change, ringing empty meaning over. A ring that ends with nobody answering and someone missing it calls missedCall. The snapshot lists an account's rings as huddleRings; rings are live, and stopping announces none.
The ready snapshot carries blocked, whom this account blocked, which also says the server blocks and takes reports (E12), and openReports for the owner and admins.

entries.plain: Creates time-ordered IDs for messages and other records, plus random invite codes and secret keys for apps.
entries.summary: Creates sortable entity IDs and random invitation/integration secrets.
details: ULID-style IDs combine a Crockford-base32 timestamp with random characters, letting ordinary lexicographic comparisons support time-ordered history paging.

Messages take orderedUlid: within one millisecond it counts up from the previous random half instead of drawing a new one, so ids sort in the order the messages were made. History pages and client lists order by id, and two messages in one millisecond used to sort either way round. Its ids are easy to guess from a neighbour, so nothing that acts as a capability uses it.
Invitation codes use a short readable alphabet; bot and webhook secrets use longer random hex tokens with an optional prefix.
An ID is a reference, while a secret token grants a specific authority. The two must not be treated as interchangeable by callers.

entries.plain: Reads an uploaded picture's width and height so the conversation can save room for it and not jump while it loads.
entries.summary: Reads image dimensions from headers without loading a native decoder.
details: PNG, GIF, WebP variants and JPEG frame headers are recognized; unsupported shapes return null.
The resulting dimensions are attached to file metadata so the client can reserve image space before decoding and reduce timeline layout jumps.
It extracts dimensions, not a proof that the whole file is a valid or trustworthy image.

entries.plain: Makes a fresh copy of the workspace for its owner to download, and unpacks a downloaded copy so it can be restored.
entries.summary: Owns the owner's downloadable copy and the zip form of a backup.
details: WorkspaceCopies keeps one copy at a time: making, ready for an hour (longer while a download reads it) or failed with its reason. A new one is refused while the ready one is being downloaded, since Windows cannot delete open files.
backupZipEntries turns a verified backup folder into zip entries with their CRCs; the server serves them through a one-shot ticket bound to the owner's session and the copy's id.
unzipBackup takes only manifest.json, workspace.db and files/<id>, also one folder down (a hand-zipped backup folder), refuses duplicates and never writes into an existing folder.
withBackupFolder lets verify-backup and restore take a .zip: unpacked beside it, used, then removed.

entries.plain: Checks a workspace's icon before it is kept: only a small PNG, JPEG or WebP picture, judged by what the file really is rather than by what it says it is.
entries.summary: Validates, versions and stores the workspace icon without decoding it (UX-60).
details: iconTypeOf reads the first bytes for the PNG, JPEG and WebP signatures. checkIcon refuses a declared type that is not one of those three (415, so SVG and its script never get in), a body over WORKSPACE_ICON_MAX_BYTES (413), bytes that are none of them or disagree with the declared type (400), and a header claiming more than 1024 pixels a side, which every client would have to decode.
The server never decodes or resizes, keeping it free of native image libraries; the client cuts the picture to 256 pixels square first. imageSize reads only the dimensions the header claims.

An icon's version is the first 16 hex digits of the SHA-256 of its bytes, so the same picture always has the same version and a changed one a new version, which is what lets clients keep it under ?v= for a year.

It is kept as three meta rows (workspace_icon_type, workspace_icon_version, workspace_icon_data in base64) rather than a table, so no migration is needed and backups and restores carry it. readStoredIcon reads them back only when they make a whole icon whose bytes match their version; the desktop app reads a stopped workspace's icon through it.
checkIcon takes a noun, so the same rules refuse a profile picture in its own words (E9).

entries.plain: Packs a workspace copy into one zip file, and unpacks one, without any outside library.
entries.summary: Writes stored ZIP/ZIP64 archives with exact lengths and reads stored or deflated entries back.
details: zipArchive lays out local headers, data and the central directory for entries whose size and CRC-32 are known first, so the length is exact (Content-Length, a progress bar) and no data descriptors are needed.

ZIP64 extra fields and end records are added only when a size, an offset or the entry count passes what classic ZIP holds (4 GiB, 65,535); a test streams a 4.3 GB entry through a virtual file to check them.
An entry that grows or shrinks while it streams stops the zip with an error. Names with .., a leading slash or backslashes are refused.
readZipDirectory finds the end record (and its ZIP64 locator) through a read function; extractZipEntry inflates deflated entries and checks size and CRC before keeping a file.

entries.plain: The front door to the server's code, which the desktop app uses to run a workspace or make backups.
entries.summary: Defines the server package's public API for desktop embedding and tooling.
details: Exports server creation/options, Store, workspace holds, backup/recovery-adjacent operations and shared security policies.
Consumers can embed a workspace server or perform offline backup operations without importing the CLI entry point and executing argument parsing.
Explicit type exports keep the package boundary readable and allow desktop adapters to depend on stable contracts.

entries.plain: Signs what the server sends to outside apps and rewrites workspace events in the form Slack apps expect.
entries.summary: Signs outbound callbacks and adapts durable native events to Slack's event shape.
details: HMAC-SHA256 signs v0:timestamp:body and emits both OwnBase and Slack header names, allowing existing receiver verification libraries to work.
Message, reaction, pin, membership, channel and user events map to supported Slack Events API payloads; unsupported native events return null.
eventActorId identifies the account behind applicable events so the dispatcher can avoid feeding a bot its own actions and creating reply loops.
Receiver code still needs to enforce timestamp freshness and deduplication; signing alone does not eliminate replay or repeated delivery.
A message.updated with previewsOnly maps to nothing (E2): a preview found or removed changes nothing an app was told, so it gets no message_changed.
So does a message.updated with pollOnly (E6): a vote or a poll closing is not something an app was told about.

entries.plain: Slows down password guessing and floods of requests, while still letting an app back from offline send its waiting messages.
entries.summary: Rations abusive workloads while allowing normal startup and offline-outbox bursts.
details: Token buckets separate burst allowance from refill per minute and key budgets by account, handle, address or webhook as appropriate.
Correct password attempts clear the handle guessing budget; loose address budgets accommodate many people behind office NAT.
Refused operations report time until retry without spending another token. Periodic sweeping removes refilled buckets so memory follows active callers.
Per-account/per-app in-flight callback caps limit slow endpoints; separate ceilings limit response URLs, triggers and open forms.
Buckets are intentionally in memory: restart permits one fresh burst in exchange for avoiding a database write on every admission.
publicByAddress (a burst of 120, then four a second) rations reads anyone may make without an account, such as the workspace icon, keyed on the address and loose for the NAT reason.

entries.plain: Starts the server on its own and runs the host's backup, restore and account recovery commands.
entries.summary: Runs the standalone server and its operator commands.
details: Parses flags/environment, validates startup values, locates the built web client and chooses LAN or isolated loopback hosting.
Dispatches backup, verify-backup, restore and local account recovery commands before ordinary server startup.
Verification prints the consequences of starting a backup: app callbacks, queued messages, accepted sessions and host settings that must be configured again.
Ordinary startup reports reachable addresses and first-owner claim information, advertises discovery when enabled and handles process shutdown.
This is an executable entry point; desktop embedding uses the library API instead.

--name, --invite-only and --access-policy set up a new workspace only. On a workspace that already has an owner the stored name and rule win, and the start prints one line for each flag that disagrees (keptSettingsNotes).
recover says when it turned two-step sign-in off (E11).

entries.plain: Announces the workspace on the local network so the app can find it without anyone typing an address.
entries.summary: Publishes a workspace discovery announcement on the local network.
details: Bonjour advertises the shared service type, port, workspace name, server/protocol versions and per-start instance ID, plus the icon's version (icon) when the workspace has one (discoveryTxt).
The server announces again whenever the name or the icon changes, so a list of found workspaces shows the current ones.
The instance ID can be compared with /api/health to distinguish the intended local server from another listener on the same port.
The returned stop handle removes the service and destroys Bonjour resources during server shutdown.
Discovery helps locate a server; it does not authenticate a person or grant channel access.

entries.plain: Works out where each connection really comes from, without believing addresses that a visitor could fake.
entries.summary: Separates trusted connection identity from caller-controlled forwarding headers.
details: originFromConnection builds an origin from the socket's local address/port, correctly bracketing IPv6 rather than trusting Host.
A loopback browser origin must match host and port for first-owner local admission; a different service on the same computer is not the same origin.
Rate-limit identity normally uses the socket peer. An explicitly trusted loopback proxy may supply a valid Cloudflare address or the rightmost forwarded hop.
Ambiguous or invalid forwarded values are rejected, and non-loopback peers cannot gain proxy trust by writing those headers.

entries.plain: Sends requests to outside apps, and reads pages for link previews, with time and size limits and, by default, keeps them off the host's private network.
entries.summary: Makes bounded outbound requests, app POSTs and link-preview GETs, while protecting the host's private network.
details: Private IPv4/IPv6 ranges and literal private hosts are blocked by default. DNS checks run inside the actual socket lookup, closing the check/connect gap used by DNS rebinding.
postToUrl follows no redirect, because a public endpoint could redirect to a private target. The host may deliberately allow private hooks for LAN bots.
Responses have a byte ceiling plus inactivity and whole-request deadlines, preventing an endpoint from holding a connection indefinitely with a slow stream.
Shutdown AbortSignal cancels calls and releases listeners; typed errors distinguish blocked, unreachable, timeout, too-large and aborted failures.

Both calls share one guarded exchange. getFromUrl (E2) follows at most maxRedirects redirects, parsing each Location against the current address and checking it as a new one, and its timeoutMs covers every hop together; with truncate, a body past maxBytes is cut there instead of refused. blocked replaces the private-range check for tests, which let loopback through and refuse the rest.

entries.plain: Finds the web addresses in a message and reads what each page says about itself, through the same guard as app requests, so a preview can show it.
entries.summary: Picks a message's previewable links and fetches each page's title, description, site name and picture through the outbound guard (E2).
details: previewLinks takes the first three web addresses in a message's words, each once, by the client's own link grammar: Slack's <url|label> and <url> forms and bare addresses, trailing punctuation and an unpaired ) left off. Code blocks and inline code, addresses with a user name or password, and links into a workspace (#/c/...) get none.

fetchLinkPreview reads a page with getFromUrl: never a private, loopback or link-local address, whatever --allow-private-hooks says, at most three redirects each checked again, 5 seconds and the first 512 KB. Only text/html or application/xhtml+xml with a 2xx status counts. readPage takes Open Graph, then Twitter, then <title> and description from the head, decodes entities, drops tags and control characters and cuts each field, and returns null when there is neither a title nor a description.

The page is decoded in the character set its Content-Type or meta tag names, through TextDecoder, falling back to UTF-8. Its picture is fetched the same way with a 1 MB limit and kept only if its first bytes say PNG, JPEG, WebP or GIF (previewImageType) and imageSize finds a header of at most 8000 pixels a side and 40 million in all; the server never decodes it. A picture that fails leaves the preview without one.

entries.plain: Makes sure only one server at a time can open and change a workspace folder.
entries.summary: Ensures one process owns a writable workspace folder at a time.
details: A small SQLite lock database holds BEGIN IMMEDIATE for the owner's lifetime before the workspace database and blob accounting are opened.
OS file locking releases the hold after a crash; no stale PID heuristic is needed. Alternate spellings or filesystem aliases reach the same underlying lock.
A separate owner description supplies useful process/host/purpose/port information when a second writer is refused; the description is not the locking authority.
release is safe to repeat. The guarantee depends on filesystem lock behavior, so a network share that does not honor SQLite locking cannot provide it.

holdWorkspacePath locks a sibling <folder>.lock, so the path stays held while restore renames folders; holdWorkspace takes it before making or locking the folder. The file is removed on release, and acquisition compares the file's identity before and after locking so a file its last holder removed is not taken for the lock.

entries.plain: Lets the host get someone back into their account with a temporary password, from the computer that holds the workspace.
entries.summary: Restores access to a human account from the machine that owns the workspace files.
details: Recovery refuses a workspace already held by a server and opens the database directly under an exclusive hold; no unauthenticated remote recovery endpoint exists.
It issues a temporary password, revokes all existing sessions, reactivates the account if needed and forces a new password before ordinary workspace use.
Optional makeOwner demotes any prior owner to admin and promotes the recovered human account, preserving a path back when an owner has left.
The changes and host-origin audit entry are transactional; handles close and the hold releases on every exit. Bot accounts are refused because they use tokens.
It also turns two-step sign-in off (E11), since whoever lost their password may have lost their phone too, and says so in its result and its audit entry.

entries.plain: Hides invite codes, sign-in keys and other secrets from the server's logs, keeping the rest of each line useful.
entries.summary: Keeps request logs useful without copying URL and header credentials.
details: Sensitive path segments cover invitation codes, incoming webhook tokens and command response capabilities. Sensitive query values include download, token, ticket, code and secret.
Authorization, cookies and signature headers are removed by logger configuration; request URLs are serialized through redactUrl.
N01 catches malformed percent encoding in a query name and masks both name and value instead of throwing before the route error boundary.
The real child-server regression verifies subsequent requests still succeed. New secret-bearing routes must be added to this explicit inventory.

entries.plain: Checks the host's settings for the servers that help huddle calls connect across networks.
entries.summary: Validates host-supplied STUN/TURN configuration for browser peer connections.
details: The schema allows bounded STUN, STUNS, TURN and TURNS URLs with optional username/credential, capped numbers of configurations and URLs.
Environment JSON is parsed once with an actionable configuration error when malformed.
The server exposes authorized configuration; peer media uses WebRTC directly or the configured relay rather than flowing through Gateway.

entries.plain: Sets up a relay, from Cloudflare, the host's own coturn or elsewhere, that carries huddle audio and video when two networks will not connect directly.
entries.summary: A TURN relay for calls between networks that will not connect directly: Cloudflare's, one sharing a secret with the server, or any other.
details: callRelaySchema accepts a Cloudflare TURN key (ID and API token) or another relay's turn:/turns: addresses, username and password, the two kinds the desktop app saves. serverRelaySchema adds a shared-secret relay (addresses and a secret of at least 16 characters), which only the environment sets.

relayFromEnvironment reads OWNBASE_TURN_URLS and OWNBASE_TURN_SECRET, or OWNBASE_CLOUDFLARE_TURN_KEY_ID and OWNBASE_CLOUDFLARE_TURN_API_TOKEN: each pair both or neither, never both pairs, refused with a ConfigError that leaves the secret out.

cloudflareIceServers asks Cloudflare's credential endpoint for a password that lasts a day, leaves out port 53 (browsers block it), and turns refusals into words a host can act on without repeating the token.

sharedSecretCredential signs a member's password as coturn's use-auth-secret checks it: username <expiry>:<userId>, a day ahead, password HMAC-SHA1 of it in base64. coturn counts quotas on the part after the colon, so per member.

createRelaySource reuses one Cloudflare password for an hour and one request for everyone joining at once; after a refusal calls go without a relay for 30 seconds before it asks again, and error() says why. A shared secret signs a password for each member as they ask. withRelay adds the relay after the workspace's own servers, leaving out an address already given.

entries.plain: Sets the safety rules a browser follows on OwnBase's pages, such as running only OwnBase's own code.
entries.summary: Defines browser and desktop content policies that fit a multi-workspace chat client.
details: Scripts are restricted to self; object embedding and framing are denied. Blob/data image and worker sources support previews and compiled assets.
Connections intentionally allow different workspace addresses because one static client may join servers other than the page host.
The desktop meta policy omits frame-ancestors because browsers cannot enforce that directive through a meta element.
No-referrer reduces URL-token leakage on external navigation; nosniff and X-Frame-Options supplement the CSP.

entries.plain: The heart of the server, which answers the app, checks who may do what, saves messages and files, and runs background chores.
entries.summary: Composes the workspace HTTP API, authorization, background work and lifecycle.
details: Creates the exclusive workspace owner, upgraded Store, Fastify routes, Gateway, attachment budget and timers. Shared validation and permission checks enforce auth, membership, roles and password-change restrictions.

Message creation atomically validates target/thread/files, checks account-scoped nonce identity, writes the message, send key and event, and completes a schedule when applicable. Fan-out happens after commit.

Event subscribers are queued inside the event transaction; per-event actor, bot membership and body work is reused across subscribers. Delivery and file-removal pumps have limits, retries and operational failure reporting.

Every change to an account's scheduled queue (queued, edited, moved, cancelled, sent, failed, or held for a new reason) sends that account's own sockets a private scheduled event, announced by scheduledEvents in the ready snapshot, so an open Scheduled list reads the queue again at once (UX-08).

Retention removes whole eligible threads in bounded passes and publishes history.removed after commit. Upload streams reserve chunks before writing so simultaneous uploads cannot exceed the storage budget.
N08 permits one callback in flight per modal ID, returns 409 view_submitting to overlap, and releases exclusion for correction/retry. A foreign account cannot consume the owner's form.

E18b: each person has one stack of at most three open views (viewStacks, in memory with the 30-minute openViews map). views.open starts a new stack and closes the old; views.push stacks on this app's stack or opens as views.open; views.update changes a view by view_id or external_id, refusing a stale hash, rationed like posting. A view_submission answer may update, push or clear; anything else closes the submitted view and those above it, and the result names closedViewIds. Only the top view can be submitted; POST /api/views/:id/close lets the person close their own. Every change is sent as view.open with the whole stack, or view.close when none is left.

E18c scopes: chat.postMessage needs chat:write, and chat:write.public for a public channel its bot is not in; a refusal is Slack's missing_scope with needed and provided, and every Web API answer carries x-oauth-scopes. enqueueSubscriberDeliveries skips an app whose scopes do not cover eventScope(type, channel kind). PUT /api/apps/:id/scopes (admin) replaces the list and logs app.scopes_changed with what was added and removed. Apps made through the API without a list get every scope.
N09 checks a pressed message's text/edit/actions fingerprint before delayed replace/delete. A missing or externally changed origin is a no-op; the same response URL can advance its own result.
Shutdown stops new work, aborts outbound requests and closes sockets/listeners/database/ownership in coordinated retryable cleanup. The library also exposes operations used by desktop hosting.

The file is an orchestration boundary with many domains; narrower modules carry SQL, crypto, networking and parsing. Callback exclusion cannot promise exactly-once business effects after an uncertain external retry.

Who may join is an access policy (invite_only, account_required, guest_allowed) kept with the legacy invite_only flag in one write. POST /api/auth/guest admits a display name alone while guests are allowed and an owner exists, rationed by address and capped at 200 live guests; POST /api/auth/guest/account converts the same identity to a member and replaces its sessions. requireUser refuses a guest any route outside GUEST_ROUTES, so new routes start closed to guests; guests cannot be put in private rooms, DMs or friendships, sign in with a password, or be promoted or reset by an admin. Turning guests off revokes their sessions and sockets.

GET /api/channels/:id/messages/:messageId gives one message to anyone who can read its conversation, guests included, for the card under a link to it. A message deleted, or under another conversation's id, is a 404, as is one in a conversation the reader cannot see.

A status can end by itself (UX-61): PATCH /api/me takes statusExpiresAt, and a new status without one drops an earlier end. One timer waits for the soonest end, clears every status due then and sends user.updated to everyone, as if its owner had cleared it; on start it clears what ended while the server was stopped.

A slash command whose app answered an error status, could not be reached or was blocked answers ok: false, command_failed, with the reason in message as well as in the private note to the channel, for the test in Apps and integrations (UX-63). Older clients read only ok and error.

The workspace's name and who may join belong to the workspace (UX-60). PUT /api/admin/workspace/name and /access-policy, owner or admin only, go through renameWorkspace and changeAccessPolicy, the same functions the desktop host's setWorkspaceName, setAccessPolicy and setInviteOnly call, so the two cannot drift. Each writes the audit record in the same transaction (the host as a null actor), tells every socket (workspace.renamed, workspace.accessPolicy), signs guests out with their sockets when they are no longer allowed, and tells onWorkspaceChange listeners. The start options workspaceName, accessPolicy and inviteOnly set up a workspace with no accounts only; once it has one, a start never puts back an older choice.

The workspace's icon (UX-60): PUT /api/admin/workspace/icon takes the image itself as the body (a scoped parser reads every type as bytes, so workspaceIcon.ts's check answers) and DELETE removes it, both for the owner and admins. One changeIcon, which the host's setWorkspaceIcon and removeWorkspaceIcon also use, writes the meta rows and a workspace.icon_changed audit entry naming type and size but never the image, broadcasts workspace.icon to everyone signed in and tells onWorkspaceChange. GET /api/workspace/icon serves it to anyone, under the publicByAddress allowance, typed from the checked bytes with nosniff and an ETag; with ?v= of the current version it may be cached for a year, otherwise it is revalidated, and it answers 404 when there is none. /api/server-info carries iconVersion so the join card can show it before sign-in.

A send can carry forwardFrom (E1). The sender must be able to read that message now: a missing, deleted or unreadable one answers 404 message_not_found. A forward with no words or files of its own passes on its original instead, and when the sender cannot read that original or it is gone the send answers 409 forward_unavailable. The forwarded id is part of the send's nonce identity.

Link previews (E2): after a send or an edit commits, queuePreviews puts the message in a queue of at most 200 worked by two fetches at a time, unless the workspace is an isolated copy or previews are off (meta link_previews). findPreviews fetches the links it has no row for, through a cache of 25 addresses for half an hour shared by concurrent sends, then in one change adds what it found and emits message.updated with previewsOnly, unless the message was edited or deleted meanwhile. Shutdown aborts fetches under way.

GET /api/link-previews/:id/image serves a preview's picture to readers of its message as the type its bytes said, with nosniff, no-store and a sandboxing CSP. DELETE /api/link-previews/:id is for the message's sender. PUT /api/admin/workspace/link-previews, for the owner and admins, records workspace.link_previews_changed and tells everyone signed in with workspace.linkPreviews. ServerOptions.fetchLinkPreview replaces the network fetch in tests.
PUT /api/messages/:id/mute mutes or unmutes a thread root for the account asking, which a guest may too, and tells only that account's devices with thread.follow (E3).

Reminders (E4): PUT /api/messages/:id/reminder sets or moves one (a time in the future, within five years, 200 per account; REMINDER_LIMITS, overridable in reminderLimits), DELETE removes one, GET /api/reminders lists them; guests may use all three. One timer is set for the soonest, and runs on starting, so a reminder due while the server was stopped comes due then; an isolated copy sets none. Coming due tells the account's devices with the message. One whose message is gone, whose account cannot read it or is deactivated is dropped instead, with reminder.removed, and a deleted message's reminders are dropped as the deletion is published.

Polls (E6): a send can carry poll, its words the question; one with files or a forward is refused (400 bad_poll), and a guest's is refused (403 guest_not_allowed), as an upload is. The poll is part of the send's nonce identity, and an edit of a poll answers 409 poll_not_editable. PUT /api/messages/:id/poll/votes replaces the asking account's choices, guests included; it is refused for a message that is no poll, a closed poll (409 poll_closed), an archived conversation, a choice past the last or more than one on a single-choice poll. POST /api/messages/:id/poll/close is for the poll's author. Both tell readers with message.updated and pollOnly, only when something changed; a vote first tells the voter's own devices poll.choices, after the commit and before the count, so a device never counts its own vote twice. /poll is a built-in the server lists but answers with 400 in_app_command, so an older client is told where polls are made.
GET /api/files is the file browser's page (E7), guests included, who see only public conversations' files.

Sidebar sections (E8): POST /api/sidebar-sections adds one (at most SIDEBAR_SECTIONS_MAX, 409 too_many_sections), PATCH and DELETE /api/sidebar-sections/:id rename and delete one (404 section_not_found for another account's), and PUT /api/sidebar-sections/order takes every one in a new order (409 sections_changed otherwise); guests may use all four, as they may star. Each change tells the account's devices sidebar.sections, and a deletion sends prefs for the conversations it let go. PATCH /api/channels/:id/prefs takes sectionId only for the account's own section.

Profiles (E9): PATCH /api/me takes timeZone, kept under its current name, and away, telling presence when away changes. PUT /api/me/avatar takes the picture's bytes, checked by checkIcon as a profile picture, and DELETE /api/me/avatar removes it; GUEST_ROUTES leaves both to members. GET /api/users/:id/avatar serves a picture to anyone signed in, guests too: 404 for a version that is not the picture's, kept for good under its version, and asked about again without one.

Missed calls (E10): postMissedCall posts the note of a ring nobody answered, as from the caller, through postMessage with call ("Missed huddle"); one postMessage refuses leaves none. PATCH /api/messages/:id answers 409 call_not_editable for one.

Two-step sign-in (E11): POST /api/auth/login answers a right password for an account with it with { twoStep: { challenge, expiresAt } } in place of a session, but only to a client that says loginBody.twoStep; an older one gets 401 two_step_required. The challenge is held in memory by its hash for five minutes and five wrong codes, with the password hash it was given for. POST /api/auth/two-step takes a code or a recovery code and gives the session, refusing with two_step_expired once the password changed or the account was deactivated meanwhile; one whose two-step sign-in was turned off meanwhile passes on the password. A right password clears what the handle spent on rate limits only once a session is issued, so it buys no more guesses at the code.

GET /api/me/two-step says whether it is on and how many recovery codes are left. POST /api/me/two-step takes the password and gives a new key and its otpauth URI, held in memory for ten minutes; POST /api/me/two-step/enable takes a first code from that key, turns it on and gives the recovery codes once; POST /api/me/two-step/recovery-codes and /disable take the password. Turning it on keeps every session. confirmPassword checks a password as signing in does, rationed by handle. Guests are refused by GUEST_ROUTES, and an app's token is no session.

POST /api/admin/users/:id/two-step/reset turns someone's off by resettable's rules, which the password reset shares: not one's own, an app's or a guest's, never the owner's, and another admin's only as the owner. It is audited as user.two_step_reset, and GET /api/admin/users says twoStep for each account.

Blocking (E12): PUT and DELETE /api/me/blocks/:id, guests included, refusing oneself (cannot_block_self) and apps (cannot_block_app). The blocker's devices hear blocks and their mention counts again; nothing reaches the blocked person but an ended friendship, as an unfriending. Unblocking sends friends again, since a request made meanwhile shows only now. Messages from someone blocked are delivered as ever, for the client to fold.

Reports (E12): POST /api/messages/:id/report takes a reason and a note from anyone who can read the message but did not write it, guests included, and the owner and admins hear reports with the new count. GET /api/admin/reports lists the open ones by message with the message itself, even from a conversation the admin is not in, or null once its author deleted it. POST /api/admin/reports/:id/resolve dismisses, removes (removeMessageWithin, inside the same mutate) or removes and deactivates its author by People's rules, closes every open report of it and records report.resolved against the author with the resolution and how many reports, never the text.

entries.plain: Checks every live message the app sends, such as typing or huddle signals, before the server acts on it.
entries.summary: Checks socket payloads at the server boundary before Gateway trusts them.
details: A discriminated union admits hello, ping, typing, huddle join/leave and signaling with bounded IDs, tokens and cursors.

Offer/answer SDP, ICE candidates and media state have explicit size and numeric constraints, keeping untrusted JSON within supported shapes. Media state takes an optional screenSound flag and an optional view (how tall the camera and the share are drawn, whole numbers from 0 to 4320), which older clients leave out.
Protocol TypeScript types alone cannot validate a remote caller; this Zod schema provides runtime enforcement without importing browser DOM types.
Validates huddle.report: counts, states and enums only, so a report cannot carry an address or arbitrary text.
Validates idle: whether the device has gone idle, a boolean (E9).
Validates huddle.decline: the conversation whose ring to say no to (E10).

entries.plain: Keeps track of how much space uploaded files use and stops uploads before they go over the host's limit.
entries.summary: Accounts for stored blobs and reserves upload bytes before concurrent writes.
details: Startup inventories regular blob files; reserve adds each accepted chunk to that file's accounting only if the total remains within the configured ceiling.
release removes all counted bytes for a blob after failed upload or successful cleanup, and storedIds enables database/blob reconciliation.
Chunk reservation permits many small uploads without pessimistically reserving the maximum file size for each.
Two uploads can each reserve part of the remaining space and both need retry; recoverable refusal is the tradeoff for never overspending the limit.

entries.plain: Reads and writes everything in the workspace's database, from accounts and channels to messages, search and who can see what.
entries.summary: Maps workspace rules to transactional SQLite records and authorized query results.
details: Owns account/session/channel/membership CRUD, per-user read/follow/save state, messages/files, invitations, audit records, integrations and durable queues. Visibility checks remain part of history and search queries.

Message hydration batches reactions, reply counts, pins and file metadata for a page instead of running one query per message. Indexed mentions support unread counts without reparsing the entire history.

Search combines safe quoted FTS terms, filename matches and structured filters. Rare terms start from matches; common terms try a newest-message window first and fill from older matches, preserving ordering and visibility.

N06 soft deletion blanks words and actions, clears associated reaction/pin/save/mention state and redacts older event copies, including file names/buttons. Event sequence records remain so reconnect order still works.
N07 markScheduledSent keeps status and message linkage while clearing text/file IDs and releasing scheduled-file holds in the message transaction.
Whole-thread purge uses a temporary ID table, retains only minimal send-key tombstones to prevent retry resurrection, queues blob deletions and redacts event/delivery copies together.

Due cleanup and app delivery queries isolate retrying/rejected rows so a failing item does not block healthy work. Follow-state revisions prevent stale authoritative echoes from replacing newer state.
Already delivered app copies and prior backups are outside active-store cleanup; the SQL rules do not constitute physical disk erasure.

Inline replies keep the message they answer (reply_to_id) and whether its author was notified (reply_ping). Hydration reads each quoted message as it now is, cut to replyExcerpt, or says it was deleted; a notified author is indexed as mentioned. Editing, deleting or purging a quoted message rewrites the quotes in its replies' logged copies too, so the log never keeps words that were taken back.

Guest sessions keep their 24-hour expiry instead of sliding; canAccess and listChannelsVisibleTo give a guest public channels only, whatever membership it might hold. convertGuest turns a guest into a member in place, and revokeGuestSessions reports the ended tokens so their sockets close.
listPins also counts every pin it would list (deleted messages and replies in deleted threads left out), so the header's pinned line can say how many from one row (UX-23).

A member's own choices for a conversation (notify level, muted, starred) live on their membership row, read in one shape by toPrefs for the ready snapshot, channel.access and the prefs route. Another member's row, and so their choices, is never touched.
deleteMeta removes a meta row, as removing the workspace icon does.

A forward keeps forwarded_from_id. Hydration reads each original as it now is, with its files, in one batch per page. Its words, files and author show only when the original is in a public channel or the forward's own conversation; otherwise the card is hidden, and a deleted or removed original says so. forwardSource answers a send's check, and reforwardEvents rewrites the log's copies of forwards after an edit, deletion or purge.

Link previews (E2): hydration reads each live message's previews in one batch per page, without the picture bytes, and leaves the field out when there are none. editMessage prunes previews of links the new words no longer have and keeps the rest in their new order; deleteMessage deletes them; redactEventRows empties previews in the log's copies. addPreview inserts or ignores; removePreview blanks a row and keeps it removed, so an edit keeping the link does not bring it back; previewOwner and previewImage answer the image and removal routes.

setThreadMute (E3) unfollows a thread and keeps its read cursor where it was, so a mention from before stays unread. autoFollowThread leaves a muted thread unfollowed when its muter replies, catching the cursor up to the reply; the root's author keeps a mute as it keeps an unfollow. Following or marking the thread unread ends the mute. A muted thread is unfollowed, so Activity, the Threads list and its badge leave its replies out, apart from mentions, which still count.

Reminders (E4): setReminder sets one or moves it, waiting again; listReminders and reminders give those the account can still reach, the list due first, the latest first, then waiting, the soonest first, each with its message; dueReminders, markReminderDue and nextReminderAt serve the timer, and dropMessageReminders a deletion.

Polls (E6): hydration reads each live message's poll and its votes in one batch per page and counts them, naming voters on each choice only when the poll is not anonymous. createPoll, pollRules, pollChoices, setPollChoices (which says whether anything changed), closePoll and anonymousPollChoices (for the snapshot, those the account can still read) serve the routes; deleteMessage deletes the poll and redactEventRows drops poll from the log's copies.

listSharedFiles (E7) lists the files on live messages one account can read, by the download rule (public, or a member and no guest), newest first by message id and then file id, and narrowed by kind (from FILE_TYPE_MATCH, so search and the browser agree; a picture is never a document), sharer, conversation and every word of q in the name, LIKE wildcards escaped. CROSS JOIN keeps files the outer loop, walking idx_files_message so a page stops once it is full; a test checks the plan.

Sidebar sections (E8): ChannelPrefs carries sectionId from channel_members.section_id. setChannelPrefs keeps a conversation in one place: a section clears its star and a star clears its section. sidebarSections lists an account's in order; createSidebarSection adds one last; renameSidebarSection, deleteSidebarSection (clearing its members' section_id and saying which) and orderSidebarSections (only the exact set) act on the account's own only.

Profiles (E9): a user row gives timeZone, away and avatarVersion only when set, so older comparisons of users still hold. updateUser sets the first two; isAway, avatar and setAvatar keep the rest, setAvatar with null deleting the bytes.
A message row's call_kind becomes Message.call, and createMessage keeps one (E10).

Two-step sign-in (E11): twoStep reads an account's key, last step and recovery codes left; twoStepUserIds lists who has it. enableTwoStep, disableTwoStep (which says whether it was on) and replaceRecoveryCodes are called inside a transaction; useTwoStepStep keeps the step a code was accepted for, and useRecoveryCode spends a code once.

Blocks and reports (E12): blockedIds, setBlocked, reportMessage (false for a second open report by the same person), openReportCount (messages waiting), openReports (grouped by message with its conversation and author, read through the message row) and resolveReports. NOT_BLOCKED leaves a blocked author out of unreadMentionCounts and activityMessages; listFriends leaves out a request from someone blocked.

entries.plain: Names the server's version and the exact code it was built from, for backups and network announcements.
entries.summary: Names the server version and exposes source identity stamped into builds.
details: A small standalone module avoids loading HTTP, sockets and discovery just to label a backup or announcement.
Built output includes revision and dirty state; source execution reports no build stamp rather than inventing one.
Version describes the release interface while revision/dirty identifies the actual source behind an artifact.

entries.plain: Tells browsers how long to keep saved copies of the web version's files, so pages load fast and updates arrive cleanly.
entries.summary: Applies cache rules that keep static delivery fast and upgrades coherent.
details: Content-hashed assets receive a one-year immutable cache lifetime because changing content produces a different filename.
HTML and other stable names use no-cache so a browser revalidates the page that points to the current asset hashes.
A missing /assets/ request returns a genuine asset miss rather than the single-page application's HTML; an obsolete JavaScript chunk should not be delivered as HTML.

entries.plain: The shared rules for finding a workspace on the local network and for building invite links that open in OwnBase.
entries.summary: Shares LAN discovery and invitation-link addressing conventions.
details: Defines the mDNS service type, default port and TXT fields including the per-start instance ID used by health verification.
The icon TXT field names the workspace icon's version; isIconVersion takes it only in the form a server makes (16 hex digits), since anyone on the network can announce anything.
hostWithPort brackets IPv6 literals correctly; isLinkableAddress excludes zone-specific and link-local addresses that ordinary browser URLs cannot use.
ownbase:// is the one deep-link scheme the desktop app registers and reads.

entries.plain: The shared rules for what a person, channel, message, file and every other workspace record looks like.
entries.summary: Defines the shared vocabulary of workspace records and feature metadata.
details: Models users/roles, room types, memberships, messages, files, actions, invitations, audits, sessions, schedules, apps and forms without coupling the server to React or browser DOM objects.

Message seq identifies its creation event; a live payload can have seq 0 until the client applies the envelope's sequence. Thread replies and channel-broadcast replies remain the same underlying message.
Follow records include revision and unread-hold state; operational status models storage, queues, retention, connections and event-loop delay.
Optional capability/metadata fields allow older servers and clients to interoperate without assuming support.
The shared 30-day send retry window aligns client automatic retries with server retention of minimal send keys after content is removed.
Role includes guest, and ServerInfo.accessPolicy says who may join; an older server omits it, which clients read as accounts only.

APP_SCOPES (Slack's names), DEFAULT_APP_SCOPES (posting only), APP_EVENT_TYPES and eventScope/eventScopes (E18c): which scope lets an app be sent each event from each kind of conversation, shared by the server's delivery filter and the Apps dialog. App.scopes is absent from servers before then.
ChannelPrefs.starred is one account's star on a conversation (UX-20). Servers before schema 40 leave it out, which reads as unstarred.
AuditAction includes workspace.renamed and workspace.access_policy_changed, with the target type workspace, recorded with the old and new value.
ServerInfo.iconVersion gives the icon's version, or null, before sign-in; it is absent from older servers. The audit action workspace.icon_changed records a set or a removal (UX-60).

Message.forwardedFrom is a ForwardReference: the original's id and conversation, and its author, words, files and time unless it is hidden (a private original forwarded elsewhere) or deleted. Servers before forwarding leave it out (E1).

Message.previews is LinkPreview[] (E2): id, the address as written, title, description, siteName, and the picture's size or null. Absent when a message has none and from older servers. AuditAction includes workspace.link_previews_changed.
ThreadFollow.muted is true for a thread this account muted and absent otherwise, and from servers before schema 43 (E3).
Reminder is one account's reminder about one message: its conversation and thread, remindAt, and dueAt or null while it waits. ReminderItem pairs one with its message for the list (E4).

Message.poll is a Poll (E6): options, each with its text, votes and, unless anonymous, voterIds; multiple, anonymous, voters (how many people chose anything) and closedAt. An option is known by its place. POLL_OPTIONS_MIN and POLL_OPTIONS_MAX (2 and 10), POLL_QUESTION_MAX (300) and POLL_OPTION_MAX (80) are the rules both sides share.
SharedFile is one file as the file browser lists it (E7): its FileMeta, and the message that shared it, with its conversation, thread, sharer and time.

SidebarSection is one account's named sidebar section (E8); ChannelPrefs.sectionId is the one a conversation is kept in, or null. SIDEBAR_SECTIONS_MAX (50) and SIDEBAR_SECTION_NAME_MAX (80) are the limits both sides share.
User.timeZone, User.away (set by hand) and User.avatarVersion are present only when set (E9); a picture is served under its version.
Message.call is a CallNotice, a note the server left about a call as from its caller (E10); kind missed is a huddle nobody answered.
AuditAction user.two_step_reset is an admin turning off someone's two-step sign-in (E11).

ReportReason (spam, harassment, inappropriate, other), REPORT_NOTE_MAX (500), ReportResolution (dismiss, remove, deactivate), MessageReport and ReportedMessage are what a report carries to admins (E12); AuditAction report.resolved records what was done.

entries.plain: Describes the updates the server sends, both the ones replayed after a reconnect and short-lived ones like typing.
entries.summary: Defines durable replay events and private/live socket messages.
details: WorkspaceEvent covers durable message, channel, membership and user changes; EventEnvelope adds monotonically increasing seq for reconnect replay.
history.removed names whole thread roots so clients can invalidate removed root/reply content and files even when history is evicted.

EphemeralEvent carries presence, typing, read/unread changes, private saves/preferences/follows, correlated huddle admission and one-user app replies/forms; these are never replayed as durable history.
ReadySnapshot describes current visible state and replayFrom, while synced marks completion. A null replay cursor replaces cached history; resync is the legacy fallback.
The distinction lets a lost ephemeral notice recover through a new snapshot without preserving private/transient UI messages forever.

Flags on ReadySnapshot (huddleReports, inlineReplies, forwards, scheduledEvents, activityThreads, threadMutes, stars, linkPreviews) say what this server does, so a client offers nothing an older server would refuse or quietly drop.
workspace.accessPolicy tells everyone signed in who may join now, and ReadySnapshot.workspaceSettings says the server takes Workspace settings' changes (UX-60). Older clients ignore the event.

ReadySnapshot.workspaceIcon advertises the workspace icon and iconVersion gives its version or null; the workspace.icon ephemeral event tells everyone signed in of a new version or a removal. Older clients ignore both (UX-60).

message.updated may say previewsOnly: only the message's link previews changed, which is not an edit (E2). The ephemeral workspace.linkPreviews tells everyone signed in that previews were turned on or off.

reminder tells an account's own devices that one of its reminders was set, moved or came due, with the message when it came due; reminder.removed that one is gone. ReadySnapshot.reminders lists them, and is absent from a server that keeps none (E4).

message.updated may say pollOnly: only the message's poll changed, by a vote or its closing, which is not an edit (E6). poll.choices tells an account's own devices what it now chose in a poll; ReadySnapshot.pollChoices holds those for anonymous polls, and is absent from a server without polls.
ReadySnapshot.sharedFiles says the server lists shared files (E7); an older one is offered no Files.
sidebar.sections tells an account's own devices its sections after any change; ReadySnapshot.sidebarSections lists them, absent from a server that keeps none (E8).
ReadySnapshot.profiles says the server keeps pictures, time zones and away (E9), and a client's idle message says whether its device is idle.
huddle.ring carries a HuddleRing as it now stands (E10); ReadySnapshot.huddleRings lists those an account is part of and says the server rings; huddle.decline says no to one.
blocks tells an account's own devices whom it blocked, and reports tells the owner and admins how many reported messages wait (E12); ReadySnapshot.blocked and openReports give both at connection.

entries.plain: Shared formatting rules for showing text exactly as typed and spotting @channel, @here and @everyone mentions.
entries.summary: Shares literal mrkdwn escaping and room-wide mention interpretation.
details: escapeMrkdwn prefixes formatting delimiters and backslashes so generated text such as /shrug is displayed literally.
broadcastsIn recognizes Slack-compatible <!channel>, <!here> and <!everyone> tokens, normalizing everyone to channel.
broadcastLabel turns wire tokens into user-facing labels; choosing who is eligible for notification remains an authorization/presence decision elsewhere.

entries.plain: The shared rules for the messages that set up a huddle, including which side starts the call so both do not at once.
entries.summary: Describes peer-call signaling and deterministic offer ownership.
details: Offer, answer, ICE and explicit camera/screen/muted/screenSound messages are plain serializable objects usable by both server and browser.

screenSound is said, true or false, only by a client with a fourth slot for a share's sound, and tells the other side it may send there. A client from before that slot never says it, and is sent nothing on it, since it would take any fourth track for the person's microphone.

view, in a media signal, says how tall its sender draws the camera and the share of the one it goes to, rounded to a few heights, and 0 for not drawn (E13b); that side then sends no bigger, or nothing. A server from before it strips the field, and the call is sized by its size alone.
Explicit media flags distinguish an active camera from a silent negotiated slot; a receiver track's muted flag alone is not evidence that frames exist.
shouldInitiateOffer uses user-ID ordering so two peers discovering each other do not both offer simultaneously.
HuddleState lists live participants. The protocol carries handshake/control state rather than audio or video bytes.
CallReport, CallCause, CandidateKind and CallLogEntry describe what a side saw of a connection and the server's call log, without addresses or SDP.
HuddleRing is a direct message's huddle ringing the people in it (E10): its caller, when it started and runs out, and who it still rings, who answered by joining and who declined.

entries.plain: Gathers all the shared rules in one place so the app and the server use exactly the same ones.
entries.summary: Exports the common protocol modules through one package entry.
details: Re-exports entity, event, REST validation, discovery, search, formatting, huddle and permission contracts.
Server, client and UI consume the same names instead of copying request shapes or subtly different policies.
Runtime helper/schema imports can affect bundling, so constants needed by lightweight consumers are kept outside schema-heavy definitions where practical.

entries.plain: Decides who can manage a channel, such as adding or removing people, with the same rules in the app and on the server.
entries.summary: Shares channel-management policy between server enforcement and UI affordances.
details: Owner/admin, creator and delegated member managers receive different management powers; active human status and room type are checked.
Delegated management ends with membership. Removing someone is not a public-room ban, and an administrator's management role does not grant visibility into private rooms.
Removal protects self, owner, admins and privileged managers according to the actor's authority; manager assignment rejects inappropriate bot/deactivated/creator targets.
Visibility must be checked separately by the server even when a management helper returns true.

entries.plain: Says how many members a workspace's plan includes, and counts the members, the same way on the server and in the app.
entries.summary: The MemberNotice shape the server sends its owner and admins, and planMembers, the count it is compared with (P5).
details: MemberNotice carries the plan's member count and, when the host gave them, its name and an upgrade address; the ready snapshot holds it for the owner and admins only.
planMembers counts people who can sign in: apps, guests (who last a day) and deactivated accounts are left out.
It is a notice, never a limit: nothing on the server refuses a join or a sign-in because of it.

entries.plain: Lets parts that live outside the server, such as the Enterprise edition, plug into it without the server ever depending on them.
entries.summary: The ServerExtension point and the command line's extension registry (P6).
details: A ServerExtension registers routes after the server's own (with requireUser, requireAdmin, requireOwner and memberCount from the server), adds a line to the workspace status, gives the owner and admins a notice in their snapshot, and is stopped with the server.

A CommandLineExtension names its flags and help; main.ts merges them into parseArgs and --help and makes the extension from them, so a setting it cannot use is refused with a ConfigError like the server's own.
The MIT code never imports an extension: a build's entry (ee/src/main.ts) adds one with addCommandLineExtension before importing main.ts.

Signing in (P9): signInMethods() goes into server-info as signIn {methods, passwords}, requiresSingleSignOn() makes the login, register, guest-account and two-step routes refuse everyone but the owner with sso_required (asked only once the password is right), and settingsPanels() is what GET /api/admin/extension-settings shows the owner.

The context also gives storage (meta keys under extension:<name>:, listed by prefix with substr, not LIKE), users (get, byHandle, create a member nobody knows a password for, joined to the public channels), startSession and publicUrl.

entries.plain: Checks an Enterprise license on the server itself, offline, and says whether it is good, in its 14 days of grace, or over.
entries.summary: Reads OWNBASE-LICENSE-1 lines: Ed25519 signatures against trusted public keys, then the claims and where they stand in time.
details: A license is claims (id, licensee, plan, members, features, issuedAt, expiresAt) in base64url JSON, signed with Ed25519 over the prefix and claims; node:crypto alone checks it.
readLicense never throws: anything that is not a license, was changed, or was signed by a key the build does not trust is invalid with a reason in words.
An ended license is in grace for 14 days, features still on (featuresOn), then expired; one dated more than a day ahead of the server's clock is refused.

entries.plain: Lists the public keys whose licenses this build accepts. The private keys are kept elsewhere, never here.
entries.summary: TRUSTED_LICENSE_KEYS, base64url raw Ed25519 public keys, empty until the first key is made.
details: With no key listed no license is accepted, and the server runs as the free edition.
A key that has issued licenses stays listed while they run, so a new key can be added without breaking old licenses.

entries.plain: Puts the Enterprise edition in a running server: the license's state, what the owner and admins are told, and which features are on.
entries.summary: The enterprise ServerExtension and its --license command-line part.
details: enterprise() works out where the license stands each time it is asked, so one ending while the server runs ends on time; has(feature) is what Enterprise features will ask.
It adds GET /api/admin/license for the owner and admins, a workspace status line, and one notice at a time: ended, in grace, ending within 30 days, or more members than it covers.
enterpriseCommandLine reads --license, OWNBASE_LICENSE_FILE or OWNBASE_LICENSE; a license that is not one stops the server at the door, an ended one does not.
It carries single sign-on (sso.ts), on while the license has the sso feature: its routes, sign-in methods, the require-SSO rule and the owner's panel.

entries.plain: Talks to a company's sign-in service the OpenID Connect way, and checks that what it sends back is really from it, for this workspace, and still current.
entries.summary: A small OpenID Connect client: discovery, PKCE, token exchange, ID token checks (P9).
details: discover() reads <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration, wants the issuer it names to be the one asked for, and https everywhere except loopback, where tests and local providers run; it picks client_secret_basic unless only client_secret_post is offered.
authorizationUrl() asks for openid email profile with state, nonce and an S256 code challenge; exchangeCode() posts the code and verifier and wants an id_token back.

verifyIdToken() checks the signature with node:crypto against the provider's published keys (RS, PS and ES algorithms, never none or HS), then iss, aud and azp, exp and iat with a minute of clock skew, the nonce and sub. KeySet reads the keys when first needed and again, at most once a minute, for a key id not seen before.

entries.plain: Single sign-on for the Enterprise edition: the owner sets it up, people link their company account or get one, and the sign-in screen gets its button.
entries.summary: The single sign-on routes, links between accounts, and the owner's settings (P9).
details: GET /api/sso/start sends the browser to the provider with a state kept in memory for 10 minutes and bound to the browser by an HttpOnly cookie; a sign-in carries the client's challenge, a link to an account a one-time ticket from POST /api/sso/connect.

GET /api/sso/callback uses the state once, wants the same browser, checks the ID token, then links the account, finds the one linked, or makes one where the owner allows it (verified addresses at the domains given). It hands back a two-minute one-time code: <public>/#/sso/<code> in a browser, an ownbase://sso link on a page for the desktop app. POST /api/sso/redeem turns it into a session only with the verifier whose SHA-256 the start had.

Links are kept in the extension's storage as sso:identity:<hash of issuer and subject> and sso:user:<id>, so changing the issuer leaves old links unused. Accounts have no email, so nothing links by one.
Without the license feature, people already linked still sign in, but nothing new is set up, linked or made, and passwords come back. The settings never send the client secret.

entries.plain: Starts the server with the Enterprise edition in it; the server bundle is built from this file.
